source.title: Observations and Open Questions in Beam-Beam Interactions

accepted.question_text: What theoretical model can explain why, during Tevatron injection with long-range beam-beam interactions and with tunes, beam separation, longitudinal emittance, and physical aperture held fixed, the beam loss rate shows a linear dependence on the opposing beam intensity and a quadratic dependence on the opposing beam's transverse emittance and chromaticity?

evidence.quote: It would be desirable to develop a theoretical model that explains the linear dependence on the opposing beam intensity and the quadratic dependence on its emittance and chromaticity but such a detailed understanding has not yet been developed.

accepted.question_text: Are the observed long-range-loss dependencies on opposing beam intensity and transverse emittance nearly universal for a well-tuned collider operating away from harmful resonances, and if so, do they also hold in the LHC, which has several long-range beam-beam interactions per turn?

evidence.quote: It is possible that these dependencies on (N, ε) are nearly universal for a well tuned machine away from harmful resonances. One machine where this could be tested is the LHC which also has several long-range interactions per turn.

accepted.question_text: How can theoretical models of beam loss based on resonance-overlap diffusion, which predict that both the diffusion coefficient and the resulting loss rate should depend quadratically on the beam-beam parameter, be reconciled with the Tevatron empirical fit in which proton losses during stores depend nearly linearly on the beam-beam parameter?

evidence.quote: Thus the loss rate should also depend quadratically on the beam-beam parameter. The empirical fit above in Equation (3) shows a linear dependence on the beam-beam parameter. Reconciling theoretical models to the empirical fits remains a challenge.

accepted.question_text: Why did KEKB achieve a maximum vertical beam-beam parameter of only 0.09 in the higher-energy ring when beam-beam simulations predicted 0.15, and what mechanisms were limiting further luminosity increase under crab-cavity operation?

evidence.quote: The maximum vertical beam-beam parameter achieved is 0.09 in the higher energy ring as opposed to a predicted value of 0.15 by beam-beam simulations. The reasons for the discrepancy and the limitations on achieving higher luminosity were under active study as of June 2010 [23].

accepted.question_text: Why was KEKB especially susceptible to chromatic coupling in the presence of crab cavities, whereas another collider such as PEP II apparently was not, despite the fact that rotational sextupole misalignments are not uncommon?

evidence.quote: It is an interesting question why KEKB was so susceptible to this chromatic coupling and not other accelerators such as PEP II, since rotational misalignments of sextupoles are not uncommon.

accepted.question_text: What quantitative theoretical model can explain why, in SPS and similar hadron-collider observations, proton losses became more sensitive to high-order resonances when the opposing anti-proton bunch emittance was reduced to nearly match the proton emittance, even though the beam-beam parameter was about 40% lower?

evidence.quote: A quantitative theoretical model to explain these observations has not yet been developed.

accepted.question_text: Why did HERA require the proton and opposing beam transverse sizes to be matched to within about 20% in order to keep beam losses tolerable, even though the beam-beam parameter there was about 0.001, much smaller than roughly 0.005 in the SPS and about 0.008 in the Tevatron?

evidence.quote: HERA also had to control the mismatch but in their case, the beam sizes had to be matched to within 20% for tolerable beam losses [13]. This stringent tolerance is at first glance harder to understand given that the beam-beam parameter was about 0.001 compared to 0.005 in the SPS and about 0.008 in the Tevatron.

accepted.question_text: Why did the RHIC pi coherent beam-beam mode appear without causing an instability even though it lies outside the incoherent spectrum and was theoretically expected to be undamped, and what damping mechanism, if any, would control this mode in the LHC?

evidence.quote: No instability was associated with the appearance of these modes, especially the pi mode, which is outside the incoherent spectrum. This runs counter to theoretical expectations that the pi mode being undamped and would therefore, in the presence of machine impedance for example, initiate instabilities [47]. This needs to be better understood especially for the LHC where much effort has been put into understanding possible mechanisms for damping this mode, e.g. [48].

accepted.question_text: What determines the critical bunch intensity above which head-on beam-beam compensation with an electron lens becomes useful, given that simulations for RHIC and the LHC indicate that the compensation helps only at bunch intensities higher than those presently problematic in operation or planned at design?

evidence.quote: The compensation works at higher values of the bunch intensity than at present used in operation in RHIC or the design value in LHC respectively. RHIC already suffers emittance growth and beam loss at present intensities. Even though the head-on collisions cause losses, the electron lens compensation does not become effective until higher intensities. What determines the critical bunch intensity above which the electron lens is useful?

accepted.question_text: For possible future LHC crab-cavity operation, how sensitive are the beams to cavity phase noise and to synchro-betatron resonances driven by dispersion in the crab cavities, and are there additional beam-dynamics limitations that detailed studies should uncover before implementation?

evidence.quote: Some issues require detailed studies such as the sensitivity of the beam to phase noise in the cavities, synchro-betatron resonances driven by dispersion in these cavities and perhaps others.

accepted.question_text: Can the crab-waist collision scheme, which has been demonstrated for flat beams by using sextupoles in the interaction region to suppress beam-beam-driven resonances, be modified so that it also works successfully in hadron colliders with round beams, where resonances involving horizontal-phase modulation are strong?

evidence.quote: It is not immediately obvious that the same scheme will also work in hadron colliders with round beams where resonances with modulations of the horizontal phase are strong. Are there modifications of this scheme that can be successfully applied to hadron colliders?

accepted.question_text: Do longitudinally flat bunch profiles in large-Piwinski-angle luminosity schemes for the LHC genuinely produce lower transverse diffusion than Gaussian bunches when evaluated in more detailed beam-beam studies, and if they do, can such flat-profile schemes remain attractive even without very large Piwinski angles and very high bunch intensities?

evidence.quote: Preliminary studies of beam-beam effects showed lower transverse diffusion than with Gaussian bunches [62]. This needs to be checked with more detailed studies. If these results are confirmed, this scheme with longitudinally flat profiles may be attractive even without large Piwinski parameters and high bunch intensities.

accepted.question_text: If the LHC operates at more than twice its 7 TeV design energy, will the beam-beam limit be set primarily by saturation of the beam-beam parameter through emittance growth, as in the first beam-beam limit of lepton colliders, or by the creation of beam tails and direct beam loss?

evidence.quote: Will the beam-beam limit be set by the saturation of a beam-beam parameter due to emittance growth (1st beam-beam limit in lepton colliders) or by the creation of tails and beam loss?
